strengths: Novel theoretical framework: First formal analysis of generalization gap between Byzantine attacks and data poisoning in distributed learning
Rigorous technical analysis with matching upper and lower bounds for poisoning case establishing tightness
Comprehensive coverage across convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex loss functions with multiple aggregation rules (SMEA, CWTM)
Insightful proof technique using co-coercivity preservation/failure to explain the gap between threat models
Numerical validation with tailored Byzantine attack showing higher empirical instability than optimal poisoning
Well-structured presentation with informative proof sketches providing intuition for technical results
weaknesses: Severely limited experimental validation: only small-scale synthetic experiments (n=15, m=1, linear loss); no real datasets or realistic federated learning benchmarks; this significantly limits assessment of practical relevance

Unclear practical significance: gap between threat models (√(f/(n-2f)) vs f/(n-f)) may be modest for typical federated scenarios where f/n is small; no analysis of when gap becomes practically significant

Looseness of bounds: gap between worst-case theoretical κ_SMEA and empirical κ̂_f suggests the bounds are not tight in practice; worst-case analysis throughout with strong bounded gradients assumption

Limited generality: results heavily dependent on specific aggregation rules (SMEA, CWTM); lower bounds for poisoning only proven for SMEA; unclear how results extend to other robust aggregation schemes; open question remains whether any aggregation can preserve co-coercivity
Nonconvex results less polished: Theorem 3.5 shows suboptimal √n dependence for f=0; restrictive requirement n ≥ (2+ν)f; upper bounds more general than poisoning bounds

Limited practical guidance: paper formalizes that Byzantine is worse but provides minimal guidance on improving generalization performance in practice; connection between theory and actionable recommendations unclear

strengths: First formal theoretical analysis of generalization gap between Byzantine and poisoning attacks, addressing an open question with empirical motivation
Strong technical results in convex case with matching upper and lower bounds (Theorems 3.2-3.3) demonstrating rigor
Well-motivated choice of algorithmic stability framework with clear justification over alternatives (uniform convergence, PAC-Bayes, information bounds)
Comprehensive coverage across convex, strongly convex, and nonconvex settings with both attack models
Numerical validation in Section 4 empirically demonstrates the generalization gap
weaknesses: Practical significance unclear: paper doesn't explain why practitioners should care about Byzantine vs. poisoning distinction when both must be defended against simultaneously; no guidance on actionable defenses

Byzantine bounds are loose with unexplained gap between theory and experiments (Figure 1), undermining the central claim of the paper; Theory-experiment gap attributed to worst-case vs. empirical robustness coefficient κ suggests bounds may be fundamentally loose

Results critically depend on specific aggregation rule (SMEA); claimed 'broad applicability' (page 6) unsupported, as tight bounds only proven for SMEA and extensions to CWTM require restrictive assumptions (1D/separable losses)

Lower bounds use artificial constructions: linear loss (degenerate), Dirac distributions, specific constraints (T≥τm for projected-SGD), and are limited to GD variants—unclear if results are fundamental or proof artifacts
Nonconvex analysis is incomplete: no lower bounds, requires f/n strongly bounded away from 1/2, and improvement over Byzantine only appears in m-dependence not primary f/(n-f) term

Fundamental unresolved issue: failure of robust aggregation rules to preserve co-coercivity (Remark D.3) is identified as source of Byzantine instability but left unresolved, suggesting algorithmic rather than analytical solutions may be needed
Dense presentation: key constants hidden in O() notation (Byzantine bound stated as O(√κ) obscuring O(√(f/(n-2f))) dependence); overwhelmingly large appendix (47 pages) makes paper difficult to parse
No experiments on realistic datasets or problems—only synthetic data with linear losses, limiting practical validation
Theorem 3.1 optimality claim relies on circular argument using [11, Theorem 7] rather than first-principles analysis

strengths: First formal theoretical analysis of the generalization gap between Byzantine attacks and data poisoning attacks in distributed learning, addressing an important open question
Comprehensive technical treatment with matching upper and lower bounds for poisoning attacks under convex objectives, establishing tightness of the stability analysis
Sound methodological framework using algorithmic stability, which provides algorithm-centric insights into how Byzantine aggregation rules fail to preserve loss function co-coercivity
Rigorous coverage across convex, strongly convex, and smooth nonconvex loss functions with careful separation of concerns
Strong numerical validation demonstrating empirical tightness of bounds with tailored Byzantine attacks
weaknesses: Limited generality: heavy focus on SMEA and CWTM aggregation rules with unclear extension to other robust aggregation schemes; acknowledged as open problem but limits scope
Practical significance constrained: stability gap most dramatic when f→n/2 (where Byzantine learning is already hard), and modest for small f where practitioners operate
Incomplete nonconvex analysis: no matching lower bounds, additional technical constraints (n ≥ (2+ν)f), and proof artifacts (suboptimal √n dependence) suggest this case is less well-understood
Presentation challenges: dense mathematical exposition with key intuitions (co-coercivity failure) buried in appendix; limited guidance on practical implications despite technical depth

Experimental validation uses synthetic data constructed to match lower bound proof; tailored Byzantine attack succeeds by design rather than demonstrating robustness of bounds to alternative strategies

strengths: First theoretical analysis proving a fundamental gap in generalization between Byzantine failures and data poisoning, with matching upper and lower bounds for data poisoning and tight bounds for f ≥ n/3
Rigorous and principled use of algorithmic stability framework, providing clearer insights than standard uniform convergence approaches with well-executed proofs
Comprehensive technical treatment covering convex/strongly convex, GD/SGD, with explicit and concrete proof sketches that clarify the role of Byzantine adaptivity and SMEA co-coercivity violation
Clear practical motivation addressing empirically observed gaps while providing constructive lower bounds that make sources of instability explicit
Generally well-written paper with good organization, though theoretical insights into why generalization differs from optimization could be emphasized more in main text
weaknesses: Incomplete theoretical results: the fundamental gap proven for f ≥ n/3 regime does not extend to f < n/3, where only Ω(γC²T·f/(n-2f)) lower bound is shown rather than the order-of-magnitude gap demonstrated for higher f. This represents a significant open question left unresolved

Limited practical validation: experiments only on highly artificial constructed instances (n=15, m=1, T=5) with linear loss functions and specific dataset structures; no evaluation on realistic datasets or standard benchmarks undermines practical relevance

Results are largely SMEA-specific with most lower bounds tailored to this aggregator, limiting generalizability; the key insight about co-coercivity violation is SMEA-specific and whether other robust aggregators could avoid this gap remains open

Artificial constructions for lower bounds using two-group honest worker configurations at boundary values (±C) and Dirac distributions don't reflect realistic learning scenarios; generalization gap (Theorem 4.2) requires restrictive m=1 assumption with artificial data distributions

Asymmetry in threat model comparison: Byzantine workers assume full adaptivity with communication observation (Algorithm 1), while data poisoning uses non-adaptive worst-case (fixed before algorithm runs), making threat model comparison not entirely symmetric

strengths: Addresses important gap between optimization and generalization in Byzantine-robust distributed learning
Solid theoretical framework using algorithmic stability analysis with distribution-free bounds
Tight matching upper and lower bounds for data poisoning case (Theorems 3.3-3.4)
Creative lower bound construction for Byzantine case with adaptive Byzantine workers
Well-organized presentation with comprehensive supplementary material
Clear empirical validation through Figure 1 and synthetic experiments
weaknesses: Main result incomplete: claimed 'fundamental gap' only holds for f ≥ n/3; for f < n/3, Byzantine lower bounds don't match data poisoning upper bounds—only numerical evidence provided, contradicting theoretical claims
Constructions are highly artificial: linear loss functions, carefully engineered data distributions, and pathological problem instances that may not represent realistic scenarios
Results limited to SMEA aggregation rule; generalization to other robust aggregation rules (trimmed mean, coordinate median) not addressed, severely limiting applicability
Generalization gap (Theorem 4.2) based on Lemma 4.1 requires restrictive assumptions (m=1, Dirac distributions except one worker)—practical relevance unclear
Only convex loss analysis; no treatment of non-convex settings central to modern deep learning applications
Weak practical validation: experiments only on synthetic data matching lower bound constructions; no realistic datasets or comparison with practical Byzantine attacks
Distributed (S)GD only; other common optimizers (momentum, variance reduction) not analyzed

Byzantine lower bound relies on strong assumptions: Byzantine workers observe all communications, adaptively craft updates, maintain feasibility constraints throughout optimization—realism not justified

strengths: First rigorous theoretical explanation for empirically observed generalization gap between Byzantine failures and data poisoning, filling an important gap in the literature
Technically comprehensive with matching upper/lower bounds for data poisoning and tight bounds for Byzantine failures in n/3 ≤ f < n/2 regime
Novel insight that robust aggregation rules like SMEA fail to preserve loss function co-coercivity, explaining the stability difference between threat models
Well-motivated use of uniform algorithmic stability providing algorithm-centric, distribution-free, worst-case analysis directly connecting to generalization
Clever lower bound construction that exploits adaptive nature of Byzantine workers and SMEA's selection bias, particularly the three-part proof technique in Theorem 3.2
Comprehensive analysis covering multiple algorithm variants (GD/SGD) and convexity assumptions with careful treatment of both threat models
Sound experimental validation demonstrating tight constant factors and persistence of gap across Byzantine worker fractions
Clear presentation with intuitive proof sketches in main text and detailed proofs in supplementary materials
weaknesses: Incomplete lower bounds for Byzantine failures when f < n/3: only achieves Ω(f/(n-2f)) without the square root, leaving an open question about the true tight bound in this regime
Analysis restricted to smooth convex/strongly-convex losses, limiting applicability to modern deep learning settings with non-convex objectives
Lower bound constructions are somewhat artificial, using simplified linear losses and carefully structured datasets; unclear whether gaps manifest in natural problems
Limited experimental validation at small scale (n=15, T=5, m=1) with tailored Byzantine attacks that may not represent practical threat scenarios
Only SMEA aggregation rule formally analyzed despite motivation to study broader class of robust aggregation rules; results for other rules only discussed informally
Gap between worst-case theoretical bounds and practical performance not thoroughly investigated; no characterization of when bounds are tight vs. loose
Open question of robust aggregation rules preserving loss function co-coercivity remains unresolved and represents incomplete narrative
Experiments use single-sample regime (m=1) differing from realistic distributed learning settings with larger local datasets
